title: ChatGPT and the rise of large language models: the new AI-driven infodemic threat in public health

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《ChatGPT and the rise of large language models: the new AI-driven infodemic threat in public health》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · sec1-p6】Starting from a background on the evolution of LLMs and the existing evidence on their use to support medical research, we focus on ChatGPT and speculate about its future impact on research and public health. The objective of this paper is to promote a debate on ChatGPT’s space in medical research and the possible consequences in corroborating public health threats, introducing the novel concept of “AI-driven infodemic.”

【Introduction · sec1-p1】“ChatGPT” is a large language model (LLM) trained by OpenAI, an Artificial intelligence (AI) research and deployment company, released in a free research preview on November 30th 2022, to get users’ feedback and learn about its strengths and weaknesses (1) Previously developed LLMs were able to execute different natural language processing (NLP) tasks, but ChatGPT differs from its predecessors. It’s an AI chatbot optimized for dialog, especially good at interacting in a human-like conversation.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《ChatGPT and the rise of large language models: the new AI-driven infodemic threat in public health》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【The evolution of pre-trained large language models · sec2-p4】Both models achieved superior generalization capabilities, thanks to their semi-supervised approach. Using a combination of unsupervised pre-training and supervised fine-tuning, these models can apply pre-trained language representations to downstream tasks.

【Large language models to support academic research · sec3-p5】Med-PaLM, a LLM trained using few-shot prompting, exceeds previous state-of-the-art models on MedQA, a medical question answering dataset consisting of United States Medical Licensing Exam (USMLE) style questions (25). The performance of ChatGPT on USMLE was recently evaluated and it achieved around 50–60% accuracy across all examinations, near the passing threshold, but still inferior to Med-PaLM (26).
